scenes.heading: Interfaces
scenes.narration: Let's explore interfaces in Go, the lightweight behavioral contracts that give the language polymorphism without any classes or inheritance.

scenes.heading: What an interface is
items: A set of method signatures — a behavioral contract
Just having the right methods is enough
scenes.narration: An interface is simply a set of method signatures that describes what a type can do, not what it is. In Go, satisfaction is implicit and structural: a type satisfies an interface just by having all of its methods, with no `implements` keyword and no explicit declaration. This lets you satisfy interfaces you don't even know exist.

scenes.heading: How a method call dispatches
steps: Assign a concrete value to the interface
Build or look up the itab
Call jumps through the type descriptor
Dynamic dispatch to the real method
scenes.narration: Under the hood an interface value is two machine words: a pointer to a type descriptor and a pointer to the underlying value. When you assign a concrete type, the runtime records that (type, value) pair and looks up an interface table mapping the methods to the concrete implementations. Calling a method reads that table and jumps to the right function — dynamic dispatch chosen at runtime.

scenes.heading: One interface, any conforming type
scenes.narration: Here Dog satisfies the Speaker interface simply by having a Speak method — there is no declaration tying them together. The announce function accepts the interface, so it works for Dog or any future type that also has Speak. When we call s.Speak, Go dispatches dynamically to Dog's implementation. That is implicit satisfaction and polymorphism in one small example.

scenes.text: An interface is nil only when BOTH its type and value are nil — a typed-nil pointer makes it non-nil.
scenes.narration: The most infamous gotcha follows directly from that two-word shape: an interface is nil only when both its type and its value are nil. Store a nil pointer into an interface and it carries a type, so it is no longer nil. This is the classic bug where a function returns a typed-nil error and the caller's check for non-nil unexpectedly fires.

scenes.text: Favor small interfaces, define them at the consumer, accept interfaces and return concrete types.
scenes.narration: The idiomatic advice is to keep interfaces small, like io.Reader or error, define them where they are used, and accept interfaces while returning concrete types. That keeps packages decoupled, testable, and easy to evolve.
